claims.statement: Early modern rationalism; founder of modern philosophy; substance dualism
*Meditations on First Philosophy* (1641), *Discourse on the Method* (1637), *Principles of Philosophy* (1644), *The Passions of the Soul* (1649)
Substance dualism: mind and body are distinct substances; mind is res cogitans (thinking thing), body is res extensa (extended thing)
Foundationalism about knowledge: all knowledge rests on indubitable foundations accessed through clear and distinct perception
Innate ideas: certain concepts (God, self, mathematical truths) are built into the mind, not derived from experience
Mechanism about the physical world: all bodily phenomena are explicable through mechanical principles
The Cogito: "I think, therefore I am" (cogito ergo sum) -- the existence of the self is indubitable even under radical doubt
The Conceivability Argument for dualism: I can clearly and distinctly conceive of myself existing without a body; therefore mind and body are distinct substances
The Trademark Argument for God's existence: the idea of an infinite perfect being must have an infinite perfect being as its adequate cause

`phil-conceivability-arg` (conceivability-to-possibility inferences originating in the Meditations), `phil-argument-reconstruct` (the Meditations as the paradigm of structured philosophical argument from foundations), `phil-thought-experiment` (the Evil Demon as the original skeptical thought experiment), `phil-modal-arg` (conceivability as guide to metaphysical possibility)

Plato (innate ideas echo Platonic recollection); Chalmers (modern conceivability arguments drawing on Cartesian patterns); Spinoza (rationalist successor who rejected dualism for substance monism); Putnam ("brains in a vat" as contemporary version of the Evil Demon scenario)
